title: Bara Lawr
subtitle: Welsh laver cakes fried in oatmeal
excerpt: Bara lawr are small patties made from laverbread mixed with oatmeal, then fried in bacon fat until crisp on the outside. They are the served version of laverbread most traditional to south Wales. Makes about 12 patties.
sourceNotes: Bara lawr (laverbread in Welsh, literally 'laver bread') describes both the cooked seaweed paste and the fried oatmeal-coated cakes that are its most traditional preparation. S. Minwel Tibbott, Welsh Fare (1976, National Museum of Wales), gives the classic method: mix prepared laverbread with fine oatmeal to a stiff paste that can be shaped, then fry the patties in lard or bacon fat until the oatmeal crust crisps. This is the form in which laverbread most commonly appears on a traditional Welsh breakfast plate alongside fried bacon, eggs, and cockles.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Shape the patties up to an hour ahead and refrigerate, ready to fry.

glossaryTerms.definition: Fine oatmeal (not rolled oats) is mixed into the laverbread paste to stiffen it enough to shape, then provides a crisp exterior when fried. The oatmeal does not mask the seaweed flavour; it adds texture and helps the patty hold together.

content.text: Bara lawr are made from prepared laverbread mixed with enough fine

to make it stiff enough to shape into small flat patties. They are then fried in bacon fat or butter until the oatmeal crust is properly crisp. The result is a different eating experience from heated laverbread alone: the crisp exterior gives texture, and the fat from the pan (ideally bacon fat) adds richness.

The oatmeal proportion matters. Too little and the patties will not hold together in the pan; too much and they taste primarily of oatmeal. The laverbread should still dominate. Start with the amount given and adjust: the mixture should be stiff enough to hold a patty shape when pressed between wet palms.

items.prepNote: prepared, from a tin or fresh pack

content.text: Put {{laverbread}} of prepared laverbread in a bowl. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper}} of black pepper. Stir in {{oatmeal-fine}} of fine oatmeal a little at a time until the mixture is stiff enough to hold its shape. It should be firm but not dry.
With wet hands, shape tablespoons of the mixture into small flat rounds about 5 cm across and 1 cm thick.

Heat {{unsalted-butter}} of butter or bacon fat in a large frying pan over a medium-high heat. Fry the patties in batches for 3 to 4 minutes per side until the exterior is brown and crisp. Drain briefly on kitchen paper. Serve immediately alongside bacon, eggs, and cockles.

items.symptom: Patties fall apart in the pan
items.cause: Too little oatmeal or mixture too wet
items.fix: Add oatmeal a tablespoon at a time until the mixture holds a shape firmly. Let the patties sit for 5 minutes after shaping before frying.

items.symptom: Oatmeal exterior burns before the patty is heated through
items.fix: Reduce heat to medium and fry more slowly. The patties are thin and heat quickly.

content.text: Bara lawr fried in oatmeal is the standard Welsh breakfast presentation. Served alongside bacon, cockles, and eggs, it belongs to south Wales, especially the coastal and mining communities where seaweed gathering was part of daily life. The oatmeal crust keeps the patties together and gives a crisp contrast to the soft laver inside. It appears at good Welsh cafes and guesthouses on weekend mornings.
